To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
SHTs have the potential to reduce energy consumption in the residential sector but that their uptake is not likely to be sufficient to meet the 1. 5°C target.
SHTs are not a ‘silver bullet’ solution for the energy challenges of the residential sector.

SHTs are unlikely to contribute to the ambitious carbon emission reductions required under the Paris Agreement and are not easily accessible to vulnerable households, thus doing little to help alleviate energy poverty.
In summary, our research is concerned with
whether and how SHTs can be designed to contribute to energy justice in the home.
the potential of smart home technologies for the transition to a more sustainable and equitable energy system.
the extent to which smart home technologies can be seen as part of the ‘sustainable energy revolution’ and how their use can be made more equitable and sustainable.

SHTs are not the silver bullet to the energy challenges in the residential sector.
SHTs are not a silver bullet for energy poverty and climate mitigation in the residential sector.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SHTs do not address key energy challenges and may in fact contribute to their persistence.

The main takeaway from our work is that
SHTs are unlikely to deliver on the energy challenges they have been framed to tackle.
SHTs are not the silver bullet solution to energy challenges in households.
SHTs are unlikely to contribute to the decarbonisation of the domestic sphere, and may even hinder it by exacerbating energy poverty and reinforcing unsustainable consumption practices.
